S.name: Cranium
S.sum: Protective vault for the brain and the framework of the face: 8 cranial and 14 facial bones joined by fibrous sutures.
a: Frontal, parietal ×2, temporal ×2, occipital, sphenoid, ethmoid; facial bones incl. maxillae, zygomatics, nasals
Sutures (coronal, sagittal, lambdoid); atlanto-occipital joint with C1; TMJ with mandible
Foramen magnum, mastoid process, external occipital protuberance, pterion
k: Head position is the top of every postural chain: vestibular and visual righting reflexes set cervical and trunk alignment.
Forward head posture increases the effective load on the cervical extensors.
t: Mastoid or periorbital bruising suggests basilar skull fracture
Eye, verbal and motor response scored 3–15 after head injury
p: Epidural haematoma after pterion fracture (middle meningeal artery)
S.rf: Lucid interval followed by deterioration after head trauma.

S.name: Mandible
S.sum: The only movable bone of the skull. It carries the lower teeth and articulates with the temporal bones at the temporomandibular joints.
a: Body, ramus, angle, condylar and coronoid processes
TMJ: synovial, with an articular disc; hinge then glide
Mandibular foramen (inferior alveolar n.), mental foramen
t: Normal ≈ 40–50 mm; under 35 mm suggests restriction
p: Mandibular fracture (often bilateral because the bone forms a ring)

S.name: Cervical vertebrae
S.sum: Seven small vertebrae forming a lordotic curve that carries the head. C1 (atlas) and C2 (axis) are specialised for rotation.
a: Transverse foramina (vertebral artery C6–C1), bifid spinous processes C3–C6
Atlas has no body; axis has the dens; C7 is the vertebra prominens
Atlanto-occipital, atlanto-axial, facet and uncovertebral joints
k: Atlanto-axial joint provides about half of cervical rotation.
Upper cervical flexion–rotation is tested separately from the lower cervical spine.
t: Extension + rotation + axial load reproduces arm pain in radiculopathy
Decides imaging after trauma in alert patients
S.rf: Bilateral limb symptoms, gait change or clumsy hands suggest myelopathy.

S.name: Thoracic vertebrae
S.sum: Twelve vertebrae forming the kyphotic thoracic curve. Each articulates with ribs, so the region is stiff in flexion and extension but allows rotation.
a: Costal facets on bodies and transverse processes; long, downward-sloping spinous processes
Costovertebral and costotransverse joints; coronal facets
k: Thoracic rotation feeds the trunk segment of throwing and gait chains.
Loss of thoracic extension shifts load to the cervical and lumbar spine and the shoulder.
t: Rib hump on forward bending suggests structural scoliosis
S.rf: Night pain, weight loss or history of cancer: consider metastasis.

S.name: Lumbar vertebrae
S.sum: The five largest vertebrae, built to carry trunk load. Their sagittal facets favour flexion and extension and limit rotation.
a: Large kidney-shaped bodies, mammillary processes, short thick spinous processes
Intervertebral discs, sagittally oriented facet joints
Lordosis; L4–L5 lies at the level of the iliac crests
k: Lumbar spine links pelvis to thorax in every sling of the trunk.
Most sagittal motion occurs at L4–L5 and L5–S1.
t: Radicular pain at 30–70° hip flexion suggests L5/S1 root tension
Seated neural tension test; sensitive for disc-related radiculopathy
S.rf: Saddle anaesthesia, new bladder or bowel dysfunction: suspect cauda equina syndrome.

S.name: Sacrum
S.sum: Five fused vertebrae wedged between the ilia. It transmits the weight of the trunk to the pelvis through the sacroiliac joints.
a: Sacral promontory, ala, sacral foramina (S1–S4 rami), sacral hiatus
Sacrotuberous, sacrospinous, interosseous and dorsal SI ligaments
k: Nutation and counternutation at the SI joints are small (a few degrees) but load-critical.
The thoracolumbar fascia crosses here, linking latissimus dorsi to the opposite gluteus maximus.
t: Distraction, thigh thrust, compression, sacral thrust, Gaenslen; 3 or more positive supports SIJ pain
Tests load transfer through the pelvis

S.name: Sternum
S.sum: Flat bone at the front of the chest made of manubrium, body and xiphoid process. It anchors the clavicles and the upper seven costal cartilages.
a: Level of the 2nd rib and T4/T5 disc; tracheal bifurcation
k: Rises and moves forward during inspiration (pump-handle motion of the upper ribs).
S.rf: Chest pain with exertion, sweating or breathlessness is cardiac until proven otherwise.

S.name: Ribs
S.sum: Twelve pairs of curved bones that form the thoracic cage, protect the heart and lungs, and move with every breath.
a: Vein, artery, nerve run along the inferior border (pass needles above a rib)
k: Upper ribs move in pump-handle fashion; lower ribs in bucket-handle fashion.
Rib cage mobility sets thoracic rotation available to the kinetic chain.
t: Anteroposterior compression reproducing pain away from the hand suggests fracture
p: Cervical rib causing thoracic outlet syndrome

S.name: Clavicle
S.sum: S-shaped strut between sternum and scapula. It is the only bony connection between the upper limb and the axial skeleton.
a: First bone to ossify, by intramembranous ossification
k: Elevates and rotates posteriorly (≈30–50°) as the arm rises overhead.
t: Pain over the AC joint suggests AC pathology
Springy distal clavicle after AC separation
p: SC joint dislocation (posterior: airway and vessel risk)

S.name: Scapula
S.sum: Triangular bone gliding on the posterior chest wall. It provides the glenoid socket and attachment for 17 muscles.
a: Glenoid, acromion, coracoid, spine, superior and inferior angles
Rotator cuff, serratus anterior, trapezius, rhomboids, levator scapulae
k: Scapulohumeral rhythm is about 2:1 glenohumeral to scapulothoracic motion during elevation.
Upward rotation needs trapezius and serratus anterior working as a force couple.
t: Manual upward rotation that eases impingement pain implicates dyskinesis
Medial winging suggests serratus anterior or long thoracic nerve weakness

S.name: Humerus
S.sum: Bone of the arm from shoulder to elbow. Three major nerves run in direct contact with it, which shapes the injury pattern of each fracture.
a: Head, anatomical & surgical necks, greater & lesser tubercles, bicipital groove
k: Internal rotation reaches roughly 7000°/s in a baseball pitch, among the fastest joint motions measured in humans.
t: Test wrist extension after any shaft fracture (radial nerve)
Lateral shoulder sensation tests the axillary nerve
p: Midshaft fracture with radial nerve palsy
Supracondylar fracture in children (brachial artery, median nerve)

S.name: Ulna
S.sum: Medial bone of the forearm. Its trochlear notch grips the humerus to form the hinge of the elbow.
a: Olecranon, coronoid process, trochlear & radial notches, ulnar styloid
k: Stays largely fixed while the radius rotates around it in pronation and supination.
t: Swelling or bogginess suggests olecranon bursitis
p: Monteggia fracture (ulnar shaft + radial head dislocation)

S.name: Radius
S.sum: Lateral bone of the forearm. It rotates around the ulna and carries most of the load passing from hand to forearm.
a: Head, neck, radial tuberosity (biceps), styloid process, Lister tubercle
Distal radius carries ≈80% of axial wrist load
k: Pronation and supination: radius crosses over the ulna, ≈80° each way.
t: Tenderness after a fall on the outstretched hand suggests radial head fracture
p: Radial head fracture; pulled elbow in children

S.name: Hand & wrist bones
S.sum: 27 bones: 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals and 14 phalanges. In anatomical position the palms face forward and the thumbs point laterally.
a: Scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform; trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate
5; the thumb metacarpal sits on a saddle joint
k: The distal link of every upper-limb chain; grip needs wrist extension to set finger flexor length.
t: Suggests scaphoid fracture even when the X-ray is normal
Pain with thumb flexion + ulnar deviation: de Quervain tenosynovitis
p: Scaphoid fracture (retrograde blood supply, avascular necrosis risk)

S.name: Pelvis (hip bone)
S.sum: Ilium, ischium and pubis fused at the acetabulum. With the sacrum they form a ring that transfers trunk load into the legs.
a: Iliac crest, ASIS, AIIS, ischial tuberosity, pubic symphysis, acetabulum
k: Pelvic tilt couples lumbar lordosis to hip position.
In single-leg stance the stance-side abductors keep the opposite pelvis level.
t: Contralateral pelvic drop in single-leg stance: hip abductor weakness
Pain on lateral compression after trauma suggests ring injury
p: ASIS / AIIS avulsion in adolescent athletes
S.rf: Pelvic fracture with hypotension: life-threatening haemorrhage.

S.name: Femur
S.sum: Longest and strongest bone in the body. Its angled neck places the knee under the body’s centre of mass.
a: Linea aspera, medial & lateral condyles, adductor tubercle
k: Femoral adduction + internal rotation is the hip component of dynamic knee valgus.
t: Shortened, externally rotated leg after a fall suggests hip fracture
Pain on passive rotation: intra-articular hip pathology
p: Femoral neck fracture (avascular necrosis risk when displaced)

S.name: Patella
S.sum: Largest sesamoid bone, embedded in the quadriceps tendon. It lengthens the lever arm of the quadriceps.
a: Quadriceps tendon above, patellar ligament below
Thickest articular cartilage in the body
k: Q-angle ≈14° in men and ≈17° in women; a larger angle increases lateral pull.

S.name: Tibia
S.sum: Medial, weight-bearing bone of the leg. Its subcutaneous front surface makes it prone to open fractures and stress injury.
a: Medial & lateral plateaus, tibial tuberosity, Gerdy tubercle, medial malleolus
Carries most (≈85%) of body weight through the leg
k: Rotates internally with subtalar pronation and externally with supination.
Screw-home: the tibia rotates externally in the last degrees of knee extension.
t: Focal pain on single-leg hopping suggests tibial stress fracture
Pain on passive stretch out of proportion: compartment syndrome
S.rf: Pain out of proportion after tibial fracture: compartment syndrome.

S.name: Fibula
S.sum: Slender lateral bone of the leg. It carries little weight but anchors muscles and forms the lateral wall of the ankle mortise.
a: Common fibular nerve wraps around the neck
k: Moves slightly upward and rotates with ankle dorsiflexion to widen the mortise.
t: Compressing mid-calf causes distal pain: syndesmosis injury
Tenderness at the posterior edge of the lateral malleolus
p: Fibular neck fracture with foot drop

S.name: Foot bones
S.sum: 26 bones arranged in three arches that absorb load at contact and stiffen into a lever for push-off.
a: Talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, three cuneiforms
No muscle attachments; covered mostly by cartilage
k: Subtalar pronation at loading drives tibial internal rotation up the chain.
Windlass mechanism: toe extension tightens the plantar fascia and raises the arch.
t: Great-toe extension reproduces heel pain: plantar fasciopathy
A drop over 10 mm from sitting to standing suggests excess pronation
Navicular or 5th metatarsal base tenderness needs X-ray

S.name: Sternocleidomastoid
S.sum: Strap muscle running diagonally across the side of the neck. It divides the neck into anterior and posterior triangles.
a: Manubrium (sternal head); medial third of clavicle (clavicular head)
Mastoid process; lateral superior nuchal line
act: One side: lateral flexion to the same side, rotation to the opposite side
Both sides: neck flexion; accessory inspiration
t: Weakness to the opposite side suggests CN XI lesion

S.name: Trapezius
S.sum: Large diamond-shaped muscle of the upper back and neck. Its three parts move the scapula in different directions.
a: External occipital protuberance, ligamentum nuchae, spinous processes C7–T12
Lateral third of clavicle, acromion, spine of scapula
t: Weakness suggests CN XI injury (posterior triangle surgery)
p: CN XI palsy: shoulder droop, lateral winging
Upper trapezius overactivity in neck pain

S.name: Deltoid
S.sum: Rounded muscle capping the shoulder. Its anterior, middle and posterior fibres act on the arm in every direction.
a: Lateral third of clavicle, acromion, spine of scapula
t: Inability to hold the arm in extension: axillary nerve palsy
p: Axillary nerve injury after dislocation or surgical-neck fracture

S.name: Pectoralis major
S.sum: Fan-shaped chest muscle converging on the humerus. It is the main adductor and internal rotator of the arm.
a: Clavicular head: medial clavicle. Sternocostal: sternum, costal cartilages 1–6
t: Pain and a palpable defect at the axillary fold: tendon rupture

S.name: Serratus anterior
S.sum: Saw-toothed muscle on the side of the chest that holds the scapula flat against the ribs.
a: Costal surface of the medial border of the scapula
act: Upward rotation of the scapula (with trapezius)

S.name: Biceps brachii
S.sum: Two-headed muscle on the front of the arm. It is the main supinator of the forearm and a strong elbow flexor.
a: Short head: coracoid process. Long head: supraglenoid tubercle
t: Resisted shoulder flexion with forearm supinated: long head pathology
Cannot hook the distal tendon: distal rupture

S.name: Triceps brachii
S.sum: Three-headed muscle on the back of the arm and the only major elbow extensor.
a: Long: infraglenoid tubercle. Lateral: above radial groove. Medial: below radial groove
act: Long head: shoulder extension and adduction
t: Weakness with reduced reflex suggests C7 radiculopathy

S.name: Rectus abdominis
S.sum: Paired vertical muscle of the abdominal wall divided by tendinous intersections into the familiar "six-pack".
t: Pain persisting when the abdominal wall is tensed points to the wall, not the viscera

S.name: External oblique
S.sum: Largest and most superficial flat abdominal muscle. Its fibres run down and forward, like hands in front pockets.
a: Linea alba, pubic tubercle, anterior iliac crest
Lower border forms the inguinal ligament
act: Both sides: trunk flexion, abdominal compression
One side: lateral flexion same side, rotation to the opposite side
t: Pain at the pubic attachment in athletic pubalgia

S.name: Internal oblique
S.sum: Middle layer of the abdominal wall, deep to the external oblique, with fibres running up and forward.
a: Thoracolumbar fascia, anterior iliac crest, lateral inguinal ligament
Ribs 10–12, linea alba, pubic crest (conjoint tendon)
act: One side: lateral flexion and rotation to the same side

S.name: Diaphragm
S.sum: Dome-shaped sheet between thorax and abdomen and the primary muscle of breathing. The right dome sits higher, over the liver.
a: Xiphoid, costal cartilages 7–12, L1–L3 via the crura
IVC at T8, oesophagus at T10, aorta at T12
act: Contracts and descends to draw air into the lungs
Raises intra-abdominal pressure for spinal stiffness
t: Paradoxical upward movement on fluoroscopy: phrenic palsy
S.rf: Shoulder-tip pain can be referred from diaphragmatic irritation (C4), for example a ruptured spleen.

S.name: Iliopsoas
S.sum: Psoas major and iliacus sharing one tendon. It is the strongest hip flexor and links the lumbar spine to the femur.
a: Psoas: T12–L5 bodies, discs and transverse processes. Iliacus: iliac fossa
Psoas: L1–L3 ventral rami. Iliacus: femoral nerve (L2–L3)
act: Trunk flexion when the femur is fixed
t: Thigh rising off the table: hip flexor tightness
Pain on hip extension: retrocaecal appendicitis

S.name: Quadriceps femoris
S.sum: Four muscles on the front of the thigh: rectus femoris and the three vasti. Together they are the knee’s only extensor.
a: RF: AIIS. VL: greater trochanter, linea aspera. VM: intertrochanteric line, linea aspera. VI: femoral shaft
Patella, then tibial tuberosity via patellar ligament
act: Rectus femoris also flexes the hip
Eccentric control of knee flexion in landing
t: Hip rises when the knee is flexed prone: rectus femoris tightness
Active extension short of passive: quadriceps weakness or inhibition

S.name: Hip adductors
S.sum: Adductor longus, brevis and magnus with gracilis and pectineus. They pull the thigh toward the midline and steady the pelvis.
a: Body and rami of pubis; ischial tuberosity (magnus)
Linea aspera, adductor tubercle; pes anserinus (gracilis)
Obturator nerve (L2–L4); magnus hamstring part: tibial nerve
t: Pain or weakness squeezing a ball between the knees: groin pathology
p: Adductor longus strain (most common groin strain)

S.name: Tensor fasciae latae & IT band
S.lat: Musculus tensor fasciae latae; tractus iliotibialis
S.sum: Small hip muscle tensioning the iliotibial band, a thick strip of fascia running down the outside of the thigh to the tibia.
t: Thigh fails to drop into adduction: tight ITB/TFL
Pain over the lateral femoral condyle at ≈30° flexion: ITB syndrome

S.name: Tibialis anterior
S.sum: Main muscle of the anterior compartment. It lifts the foot and controls its lowering after heel strike.
a: Lateral tibial condyle and upper lateral tibia, interosseous membrane
Medial cuneiform and base of 1st metatarsal
act: Eccentric control of foot lowering at heel strike
t: Inability suggests L4–L5 or deep fibular weakness

S.name: Fibularis longus
S.sum: Lateral leg muscle whose tendon passes behind the lateral malleolus and under the foot like a stirrup.
a: Head and upper two-thirds of lateral fibula
Medial cuneiform and base of 1st metatarsal (plantar side)
t: Weakness after sprain; also tests superficial fibular nerve

S.name: Gastrocnemius
S.sum: Two-headed calf muscle crossing both knee and ankle. It joins soleus to form the Achilles tendon.
t: No plantarflexion on calf squeeze: Achilles rupture
More dorsiflexion with knee bent: isolated gastrocnemius tightness

S.name: Gluteus maximus
S.sum: Largest muscle of the body. It extends the hip for climbing, rising and sprinting, and joins the posterior oblique sling.
a: Posterior ilium, dorsal sacrum and coccyx, sacrotuberous ligament, thoracolumbar fascia
act: Tensions the ITB to steady the knee
t: Delayed gluteal firing relative to hamstrings or erectors
Endurance and control of hip extension

S.name: Gluteus medius
S.sum: Fan-shaped hip abductor on the outer ilium. It keeps the pelvis level each time you stand on one leg.
a: External ilium between anterior and posterior gluteal lines
t: Opposite pelvis drops in single-leg stance
Knee valgus and pelvic drop reveal weak control

S.name: Hamstrings
S.sum: Biceps femoris, semitendinosus and semimembranosus. They cross hip and knee and decelerate the swinging leg in sprinting.
a: Ischial tuberosity (biceps femoris short head: linea aspera)
BF: fibular head. ST: pes anserinus. SM: posteromedial tibial condyle
Sciatic: tibial division (BF short head: common fibular)
act: BF rotates tibia outward; medial hamstrings rotate it inward
t: Pain near the ischial tuberosity: proximal tendinopathy
p: Hamstring strain (BF long head most common)

S.name: Latissimus dorsi
S.sum: Broad flat muscle of the back linking the pelvis and spine to the arm through the thoracolumbar fascia.
a: Spinous processes T7–T12, thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest, ribs 9–12
t: Arm fails to reach the table with lumbar spine flat: lat tightness

S.name: Erector spinae
S.sum: Iliocostalis, longissimus and spinalis columns running the length of the spine. They extend it and control forward bending.
a: Common tendon from sacrum, iliac crest and lumbar spinous processes
Ribs, transverse and spinous processes, mastoid process
act: One side: lateral flexion to the same side
t: Trunk extensor endurance; under ≈176 s is associated with low back pain risk in men
Absent in many people with chronic low back pain

S.name: Quadratus lumborum
S.sum: Deep quadrilateral muscle between the 12th rib and the iliac crest that hitches the pelvis and side-bends the trunk.
t: Lateral trunk endurance and side-to-side symmetry

S.name: Brain
S.sum: Cerebrum, diencephalon, brainstem and cerebellum. It weighs ≈1.3–1.4 kg and receives about 15% of cardiac output.
a: Frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital lobes; brainstem; cerebellum
Circle of Willis (internal carotids + vertebrobasilar system)
Corticospinal tract crosses at the medullary pyramids
k: Sets the motor plan: proximal-to-distal timing in a throw is centrally programmed.
t: Face, arm, speech, time: stroke screen
Up-going toe: upper motor neuron lesion
S.rf: Sudden weakness, speech loss or worst-ever headache needs emergency care.

S.name: Spinal cord
S.sum: Runs from the foramen magnum to the conus medullaris at about L1–L2 in adults. Below that, nerve roots continue as the cauda equina.
k: Central pattern generators in the cord contribute to the rhythm of gait.
t: Thumb flexion on flicking the middle finger: cervical myelopathy
Rhythmic beats on rapid ankle dorsiflexion: UMN lesion
Electric shock down the spine on neck flexion
S.rf: Saddle anaesthesia with urinary retention: cauda equina syndrome.

S.name: Brachial plexus
S.sum: Network formed by the C5–T1 ventral rami in the neck and axilla. It supplies all motor and most sensory nerves of the upper limb.
a: Lateral, posterior, medial (named around the axillary artery)
k: Neural tissue must slide and lengthen through the whole arm during overhead reach.
t: Arm symptoms during 3 min of overhead hand pumping: thoracic outlet
p: Klumpke palsy (C8–T1: claw hand, Horner syndrome)

S.name: Median nerve
S.sum: Runs down the centre of the arm and forearm and through the carpal tunnel. It controls precise thumb movement.
a: With brachial artery; between pronator teres heads; under FDS; carpal tunnel
Most forearm flexors; thenar muscles; lumbricals 1–2
k: Tensioned by wrist and finger extension with elbow extension and shoulder abduction.
t: Wrist flexion for 60 s reproduces tingling
Direct pressure over the carpal tunnel

S.name: Ulnar nerve
S.sum: Passes behind the medial epicondyle (the "funny bone") and powers most small muscles of the hand.
a: Cubital tunnel; flexor carpi ulnaris; Guyon canal
FCU, medial FDP, interossei, hypothenar, adductor pollicis
k: Lengthens markedly with elbow flexion, which is why sleeping with bent elbows aggravates it.
t: Thumb IP flexion when pinching paper: adductor pollicis weakness
Symptoms after 60 s of full elbow flexion

S.name: Radial nerve
S.sum: Spirals around the back of the humerus and supplies every extensor of the elbow, wrist and fingers.
a: Radial groove of humerus; anterior to lateral epicondyle; splits into superficial and deep branches
Triceps, brachioradialis, wrist and finger extensors, supinator
Posterior arm & forearm; dorsal first web space
k: Wrist extension sets finger flexor length for a strong grip: radial palsy weakens grip too.
t: Wrist drop with radial nerve palsy
p: "Saturday night palsy" (arm draped over a chair)

S.name: Femoral nerve
S.sum: Largest branch of the lumbar plexus. It passes under the inguinal ligament lateral to the femoral artery to power the quadriceps.
a: Through psoas; under inguinal ligament (NAVeL: nerve, artery, vein, lymphatics, lateral to medial)
Anterior thigh; saphenous branch to medial leg and foot
k: Knee extension depends entirely on this nerve.
t: Anterior thigh pain: femoral nerve / upper lumbar root tension
Reduced in femoral neuropathy or L4 radiculopathy

S.name: Sciatic nerve
S.sum: Largest nerve in the body. It leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen and splits into tibial and common fibular nerves above the knee.
a: Below piriformis (usually); deep to gluteus maximus; posterior thigh
Hamstrings, adductor magnus (part), all muscles below the knee
Most of leg and foot except the medial side
k: Tensioned by hip flexion, knee extension and ankle dorsiflexion together.
t: Flexion, adduction, internal rotation: piriformis syndrome

S.name: Common fibular nerve
S.sum: Winds around the fibular neck just under the skin, the most commonly injured nerve of the lower limb.
a: Superficial (eversion, dorsum of foot) and deep (dorsiflexion, first web space)
k: Loss of dorsiflexion forces a high-stepping gait to clear the toes.
t: Weak dorsiflexion and eversion with normal inversion points to the nerve, not L5
Tapping reproduces tingling down the leg
p: Foot drop from fibular neck fracture, tight cast or leg crossing

S.name: Heart
S.sum: Four-chambered pump sitting behind the sternum with its apex toward the left. It moves about 5 L of blood per minute at rest.
a: SA node → AV node → bundle of His → Purkinje fibres
Left anterior descending, circumflex, right coronary artery
k: Cardiac output can rise 4–6× in exercise; it sets the ceiling for endurance work.
t: Aortic 2nd R ICS; pulmonic 2nd L ICS; tricuspid L lower sternal border; mitral apex
S.rf: Chest pain spreading to the left arm or jaw with sweating: call emergency services.

S.name: Aorta
S.sum: Main artery of the body. It rises from the left ventricle, arches to the left and descends in front of the spine to split at L4.
a: Brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, left subclavian
L4, near the umbilicus, into the common iliac arteries
k: Its elastic wall stores energy in systole and keeps blood moving in diastole.
t: Expansile pulsatile mass above the umbilicus: aneurysm
A large difference between arms suggests dissection
S.rf: Tearing chest or back pain: suspect dissection.

S.name: Common carotid artery
S.sum: Main artery of the head and neck. It runs beside the trachea and splits into internal and external carotids at about C4.
a: Right: brachiocephalic trunk. Left: aortic arch
S.rf: Transient one-sided vision loss or weakness: urgent vascular assessment.

S.name: Brachial artery
S.sum: Continuation of the axillary artery down the arm. It divides into radial and ulnar arteries in the cubital fossa.
a: Subclavian → axillary (1st rib) → brachial (teres major) → radial & ulnar
Medial to biceps tendon, lateral to median nerve
t: Checks radial and ulnar supply to the palmar arches
Lateral to flexor carpi radialis at the wrist

S.name: Femoral artery
S.sum: Main artery of the leg. It enters the thigh at the mid-inguinal point and becomes the popliteal artery behind the knee.
a: External iliac artery, below the inguinal ligament
Femoral triangle → adductor canal → adductor hiatus → popliteal
Profunda femoris; below knee: anterior & posterior tibial
Femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, dorsalis pedis
t: Pallor on elevation, rubor on dependency: severe ischaemia
S.rf: Pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis: acute limb ischaemia.

S.name: Lungs
S.sum: Paired organs of gas exchange. The right lung has three lobes; the left has two and a notch for the heart.
a: Right: upper, middle, lower. Left: upper (with lingula), lower
Rises 2–3 cm above the medial clavicle
k: Breathing mechanics share muscles with trunk stability (diaphragm, obliques).
t: Dull over fluid or consolidation, hyper-resonant over pneumothorax
Increased in consolidation, reduced with effusion
p: Pneumonia (aspiration favours the right lower lobe)
S.rf: Sudden breathlessness with tracheal deviation: tension pneumothorax.

S.name: Liver
S.sum: Largest internal organ (≈1.5 kg), tucked under the right ribs. It handles metabolism, bile, detoxification and plasma proteins.
a: Glycogen storage, bile, albumin and clotting factors, drug metabolism
t: Inspiration stops on RUQ pressure: gallbladder inflammation
Percussion at the midclavicular line, ≈6–12 cm
S.rf: Right shoulder pain can be referred from the liver or gallbladder via the phrenic nerve.

S.name: Stomach
S.sum: J-shaped muscular sac in the left upper abdomen that stores food and begins protein digestion with acid and pepsin.
S.rf: Vomiting blood or black stools: upper GI bleed.

S.name: Kidneys
S.sum: Bean-shaped filters lying against the posterior abdominal wall from T12 to L3. The right sits a little lower because of the liver.
t: Fist percussion at the CVA: pyelonephritis
S.rf: Flank pain with fever and rigors: pyelonephritis or obstructed infected kidney.

S.name: Intestines
S.sum: Small intestine (≈6–7 m) for digestion and absorption, framed by the large intestine (≈1.5 m) that reclaims water.
a: Caecum, appendix, ascending, transverse, descending, sigmoid colon, rectum
Villi and microvilli multiply absorptive area
t: Tenderness one-third from ASIS to umbilicus: appendicitis

S.name: Shoulder (glenohumeral)
S.sum: The most mobile joint in the body. A small glenoid holds a large humeral head, so stability comes mainly from the rotator cuff.
a: Glenoid labrum, capsule, glenohumeral & coracohumeral ligaments
Rotator cuff: supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis
t: Pain on forced IR at 90° flexion: subacromial pain
IR loss over 20° vs the other side in throwers

S.name: Elbow
S.sum: Three joints in one capsule: humeroulnar and humeroradial hinges plus the proximal radioulnar pivot.
t: Pain at 70–120° flexion: UCL injury in throwers
Resisted wrist extension: lateral elbow tendinopathy
Unable to fully extend after trauma: X-ray

S.name: Wrist
S.sum: Radiocarpal and midcarpal joints between forearm and hand, moving in two planes.
a: Distal radius and TFCC with scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum

S.name: Hip
S.sum: Deep, stable ball-and-socket joint carrying several times body weight in running.
a: Iliofemoral (Y ligament, strongest in the body), pubofemoral, ischiofemoral
t: Flexion, adduction, IR reproduces groin pain: FAI or labral tear
Flexion, abduction, ER: hip or SIJ pain

S.name: Knee
S.sum: Largest joint in the body: tibiofemoral and patellofemoral joints held by four main ligaments and two menisci.
a: Medial (C-shaped, attached to MCL), lateral (more mobile)
Tibia rotates outward in the last ≈30° of extension

S.name: Ankle
S.sum: Talocrural hinge for dorsiflexion and plantarflexion, working with the subtalar joint below it for inversion and eversion.

S.name: Cervical spine (motion)
S.sum: Combined motion of the cervical segments, the most mobile region of the spine.
a: Extension and lateral flexion limited first
t: Relief of arm pain on traction supports root compression
C1–C2 rotation under 32° points to cervicogenic headache

S.name: Lumbar spine (motion)
S.sum: Combined motion of L1–S1. Sagittal facets allow bending forward and back but little twisting.
a: Disc + two facet joints per level
t: Centralisation of pain predicts good prognosis
Pain eases when the extensors are activated
Under 5 cm increase on flexion: reduced mobility (e.g. axial spondyloarthritis)

CHAINS.name: Posterior oblique sling
seq: Loads the thoracolumbar fascia from above
Fascia crosses the midline and compresses the SI joint
CHAINS.fn: Couples one arm with the opposite hip. It creates force closure of the sacroiliac joint and transfers rotational power in gait, throwing and swimming.
dys: Gluteal inhibition shifts extension load to hamstrings and lumbar erectors
SIJ pain with poor load transfer
Reduced arm swing and trunk counter-rotation

CHAINS.name: Anterior oblique sling
seq: Stabilises the opposite hip and pelvis
CHAINS.fn: Links one side of the ribcage to the opposite thigh. It drives trunk rotation and flexion and stabilises the pelvis when changing direction, kicking and sprinting.
dys: Poor rotational control in cutting sports

CHAINS.name: Deep longitudinal sling
CHAINS.fn: Runs from the foot to the spine. It pre-tensions before heel strike, compresses the SI joint and absorbs ground reaction force.
dys: SIJ pain with reduced force closure

CHAINS.name: Lateral sling
seq: Opposite QL holds the pelvis level
CHAINS.fn: Controls the pelvis in the frontal plane during single-leg stance, walking, stair climbing and lateral cutting.

CHAINS.name: Superficial back line
CHAINS.fn: A continuous line from the sole of the foot over the back of the body to the brow. It keeps the body upright and resists forward bending.
dys: Plantar heel pain with tight calves and hamstrings

CHAINS.name: Superficial front line
CHAINS.fn: Runs up the front of the body and balances the back line. It flexes the trunk and hips, extends the knee and protects the front of the body.
dys: Anterior pelvic tilt with tight hip flexors

CHAINS.name: Dynamic knee valgus
seq: Weak hip abductors fail to resist
CHAINS.fn: A collapse pattern seen in squatting, landing and running. Look at each link: the fault can start at the foot, the hip, or both.
dys: ITB syndrome and medial tibial stress syndrome

CHAINS.name: Overhead throwing chain
seq: Drive leg pushes into the ground
Obliques transfer rotation to the thorax
CHAINS.fn: Energy flows from the ground through legs and trunk to the arm. Legs and trunk generate about half of the kinetic energy delivered to the ball.
dys: Proximal deficits make the shoulder and elbow "catch up", overloading them
